title: Backyard Evidence Lab
description: Read small invented observation tables, sort what they support from what needs an experiment, order field-note steps, and match clues to their evidence type.

sections.title: Read the clues
sections.description: Choose what each table or note really supports.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.description: Put investigation steps in a valid order.

sections.title: Sort the evidence
sections.description: Match clues and claims to what they show.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is directly supported by this woodlice count table?
questions.context: Invented data, woodlice counted under boxes on five days. Sheltered boxes: 12, 15, 11, 14, 13. Open boxes: 4, 6, 3, 5, 7.

options.label: Sheltered boxes had more woodlice than open boxes on every counted day.
Open boxes had more woodlice on at least one day.
Woodlice prefer damp spots, as this table measured dampness.
Shelter proves woodlice are attracted to boxes everywhere.

questions.explanation: Each day's sheltered count beats the open count. The table did not measure dampness, and one yard cannot prove a rule for everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which statement would need an experiment rather than more of the same observations?
questions.context: Invented lawn log of clover cover and bee visits in ten minutes. Patch A: 40% clover, 18 visits. Patch B: 10%, 5. Patch C: 25%, 11. Patch D: 5%, 3.

options.label: Patches with more clover had more bee visits in this log.
Patch D had the fewest visits.
Adding clover to a patch would raise its bee visits.
Visit counts differed between the four patches.

questions.explanation: The other statements describe the log. Claiming that adding clover changes visits is a cause-and-effect claim, so clover must be deliberately changed while other things stay the same.

questions.prompt: What does this garden log fail to separate?
questions.context: Invented log: sparrow counts were higher on every day the birdbath was full. The birdbath was only filled on days when seed was also scattered nearby.

options.label: Whether the full birdbath or the scattered seed accounts for higher counts.
Whether any days had sparrow counts recorded.
Whether seed was ever scattered on a counted day.
Whether counts differed from day to day.

questions.explanation: Water and seed always changed together, so they are confounded. Testing each alone on different days would help separate them.

questions.prompt: Rae checked one flowerpot on one afternoon: two ants under the left edge, none under the right. What is supported?

options.label: Under that pot on that afternoon, ants were found only at the left edge.
Ants always avoid the right side of pots.
Ants prefer the left side of every pot.
The right edge is unsuitable for ants.

questions.explanation: One pot at one time supports only a description of that check. General rules or reasons need repeated counts across pots and times.

questions.prompt: Order this plan from first noticing to measuring, keeping each step after what it depends on.
questions.context: Invented example: bean seedlings near a fence look taller than those by the open path.

items.label: Notice that seedlings near the fence look taller
Ask whether more sunlight could explain the height
Grow matching seeds in sunny and shaded pots with the same soil and water
Measure and compare the heights after the same number of days

questions.explanation: Observation leads to a question, the question leads to a fair test, and measurements come only after the test has run.

questions.prompt: Order this chalk-fading test. Two preparation steps may swap, but both must precede comparing results.
questions.context: Invented example: chalk marks seem to fade sooner on a sunny wall than on a shady wall.

items.label: Notice chalk fading sooner on the sunny wall
Write the question: does sun exposure change fade time?
Draw identical chalk lines on sunny and shady sections
Decide on a 0 to 3 fade rating scale
Rate and compare the lines after one day

questions.explanation: The question guides the test. Drawing lines and choosing a rating scale are independent preparation steps, but both must be done before rating.

questions.prompt: Match each woodlouse note to its type of evidence.
questions.context: Invented notes from a board-flipping check: no animals were handled.

left.label: Tally of 14 woodlice under one board
Idea that dampness draws woodlice to boards
Wet and dry paper in matching trays, placement chosen by coin flip
Note that the board was cool and shaded at noon

questions.explanation: Counts and conditions that were recorded are observations. The dampness idea is a hypothesis, and deliberately varying wetness with matched trays is an experiment.

questions.prompt: Match each claim to what the feeder table supports.
questions.context: Invented counts of feeder visits on four mornings, similar weather. Hedge feeder: 9, 7, 8, 10. Open feeder: 3, 4, 2, 3.

left.label: The hedge feeder had more visits on each morning.
Hedge cover causes birds to choose a feeder.
The open feeder will get fewer than 5 visits next month.
The hedge feeder had 34 visits in total.

questions.explanation: The table directly shows the daily comparison and the total of 34. A forecast needs future data, and a cause claim needs a deliberate change in cover.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All tables, counts and garden scenarios here are invented for practice and are not real field data. No animal handling is needed to play.

title: Moon Mission Control
description: Play flight controller across eight calls: sequence launch steps, solve transit problems, and match return constraints to reasons, then check your accuracy and read the explanations.

sections.title: Launch calls
sections.description: Sequence steps and check the mission profile.

sections.title: Transit problems
sections.description: Choose the best response.

sections.title: Return puzzles
sections.description: Match constraints to reasons.

questions.prompt: Put the invented Mission Lark pad steps in an order that respects every rule.
questions.context: Mission Lark is an invented spacecraft. Rules: the hatch leak check needs the crew already aboard. Liftoff needs both a passed leak check and finished fuel loading. Fuel loading can happen any time before liftoff.
questions.explanation: Boarding must precede the leak check, and liftoff must follow both the check and fueling. Fueling is independent, so it may come first, second or third.

questions.prompt: After Lark reaches space, order these steps so every dependency is satisfied.
questions.context: Invented rules: the health check needs solar arrays deployed. The departure burn needs a passed health check. The Moon flyby happens only after the burn. The crew photo session needs only deployed arrays.
questions.explanation: Arrays, health check, burn and flyby form one chain. The photo session only needs arrays, so it can slot in anywhere after step one.

questions.prompt: NASA's Artemis II launched April 1, 2026 with four astronauts. What was its mission profile?

options.label: A crewed loop around the Moon, without landing
A crewed landing on the lunar surface
A permanent crewed station in lunar orbit

questions.explanation: Artemis II sent Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen around the Moon and back, returning April 10. It did not land.

questions.prompt: Why might a plan loop the Moon and head home instead of orbiting first? Pick the best reason in this model.
questions.context: Simplified model: a looping path lets the Moon's gravity bend the craft back toward Earth with no big extra burn. Orbiting first needs one braking burn to enter orbit and another burn to leave.

options.label: It avoids two large burns, so it uses less fuel
It lets the craft skip heat protection on return
It makes the Moon's gravity stop acting on the craft
It guarantees longer time in lunar shadow

questions.explanation: In this model the loop saves the entering and leaving burns, since gravity does the turning. Heat protection and gravity are unaffected by the path choice.

questions.prompt: A trainee says a crescent Moon is Earth's shadow covering part of it. What is the best correction?

options.label: Phases show how much of the sunlit half we see
Phases are caused by clouds on the Moon
A crescent means Earth's shadow is thin
Phases only change when the Moon is closer

questions.explanation: Moon phases are the changing view of the Moon's sunlit portion. Earth's shadow falling on the Moon is a different event, a lunar eclipse.

questions.prompt: Lark will spend 5 shaded hours with no solar power. Which plan keeps the required reserve?
questions.context: Invented numbers: battery holds 45 units and must keep a 12-unit reserve. Essential systems use 6 units per hour. The science camera adds 4 units per hour while on.

options.label: Camera on for 2 hours, then off

questions.explanation: Usable energy is 45 minus 12, so 33 units. Essentials alone use 30. Even one camera hour brings the total to 34, over budget.

questions.prompt: Match each return constraint to the reason a planner would include it.
questions.context: Simplified model of a capsule returning to Earth at very high speed. Choose the reason that most directly explains each constraint.

left.label: Reentry angle must stay in a narrow corridor
Recovery ships wait near the landing zone
Heat shield covers the capsule's front

right.label: Too steep stresses the capsule; too shallow may skip off
Crew can be reached soon after landing
Air compressed at high speed creates intense heat

questions.explanation: The corridor balances stress against skipping, ships shorten the wait for recovery, and the shield handles heating from fast, compressed air in front of the capsule.

questions.prompt: Sort these return-cargo measurements by the kind of quantity each one describes.
questions.context: Invented manifest entries. Several entries can share the same quantity type.
questions.explanation: Kilograms and grams measure mass, meters measure length, and liters measure volume. These are different dimensions, so their numbers cannot be compared directly.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data
NASA: Moon phases
NASA: Artemis II
NIST: everyday estimation

note: Mission Lark, its checklists, battery numbers and cargo manifest are invented simplified models for puzzles, not real flight rules. Only the Artemis II and Moon phase facts come from NASA.

title: Scale Shock
description: Sort invented specimen cards by size after converting mixed units, then answer four scale-bar and size-comparison questions.

sections.title: Size Order
sections.description: Convert units and sort smallest to largest.

sections.title: Scale Checks
sections.description: Read units, scale bars and ratios.

questions.prompt: Order these four grains from smallest to largest diameter.
questions.context: These specimen cards are invented for this quiz. Each lists a measured diameter in a different length unit.
questions.explanation: Converted to millimetres: Birch 0.25, Cedar 0.3, Alder 0.4, Dune 0.5. Matching units is the key step before comparing.

questions.prompt: Sort these four invented seed pods from smallest to largest width.
questions.context: Invented specimen cards. Widths are recorded with different units.
questions.explanation: In millimetres: Reed 8, Thyme 9.5, Sage 11, Quill 12. Centimetres, metres and micrometres all convert to the same length scale.

questions.prompt: Order these four invented hill heights from lowest to highest.
questions.context: Invented survey cards for a made-up hill range. Heights use different length units.
questions.explanation: In metres: Mesa 1,750, Bluff 1,850, Ridge 1,900, Crest 2,000. The huge millimetre number is simply 2,000 m.

questions.prompt: Order these four invented pebble samples from lightest to heaviest.
questions.context: Invented lab cards. Mass is recorded in different units: 1 kg is 1,000 g, 1 g is 1,000 mg, and 1 tonne is 1,000 kg.
questions.explanation: In grams: Birch 420, Cedar 430, Dune 440, Alder 450. Converting everything to one mass unit makes the order clear.

questions.prompt: A specimen card lists four measurements. Which one is a length, suitable for a diameter?
questions.context: Card entries: 12 g, 3 mL, 40 mm, 2 cm³.
questions.explanation: Millimetres measure length. Grams measure mass, while millilitres and cubic centimetres both measure volume, so they cannot be diameters.

questions.prompt: Using the scale bar, what is the real width of the drawn specimen?
questions.context: In an invented diagram, a scale bar 2 cm long represents 5 mm in real life. The specimen is drawn 6 cm wide.
questions.explanation: The drawing is 3 times the scale bar length, so the real width is 3 × 5 mm = 15 mm.

questions.prompt: How many times wider is the 0.5 mm model grain than the 0.02 mm model cell?
questions.context: Both are invented teaching models, measured across their widest point.
questions.explanation: Divide 0.5 by 0.02 to get 25. Same-unit ratios show scale differences better than the raw numbers do.

questions.prompt: Which invented bead is larger, and by how much?
questions.context: Bead one is 1,200 µm across. Bead two is 0.9 mm across.
questions.explanation: 1,200 µm equals 1.2 mm. That is 0.3 mm more than the 0.9 mm bead.

sources.label: NIST: everyday estimation
Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All specimens, hills, beads and diagrams are invented for this quiz, and every measurement you need is given in the question. The unit relationships follow standard metric definitions.

title: Weather Without the Forecast
description: Read invented pressure logs, cloud sequences and wind shifts, then pick the change that best fits, order clue-to-outcome chains, and choose what to watch next.

sections.title: Read the sky
sections.description: Three clue sets, one best-fitting change each.

sections.title: Clue to outcome chains
sections.description: Order and match causes and outcomes.

sections.title: What to watch next
sections.description: Handle mixed evidence and choose useful readings.

questions.prompt: Given the pressure trend and cloud sequence, which change best fits the evidence?
questions.context: Invented station log, mid-latitude Northern Hemisphere. Pressure: 06:00 1018 hPa, 09:00 1015, 12:00 1012, 15:00 1009. Cloud: wispy high streaks, then a milky veil, then a lowering gray layer. Model rule: steady pressure fall with thickening, lowering cloud supports an approaching front.

options.label: Steady rain is likely to arrive later
Skies are likely to clear and dry out
A clear, calm night is likely to follow

questions.explanation: Both clues point the same way: pressure is falling and cloud is thickening and lowering, which in this model signals an approaching front and precipitation.

questions.prompt: Which change does this wind and temperature record best fit?
questions.context: Invented log, Northern Hemisphere. 14:00 wind southwest, 21°C, pressure falling. 15:10 wind abruptly northwest, 15°C, then pressure begins rising. Model rule: an abrupt wind shift to northwest with sharp cooling and a pressure turnaround marks a cold front passing.

options.label: A cold front has just passed, bringing cooler air
A warm front is still hours away
The air mass is stalling and warming
Pressure is falling more quickly now

questions.explanation: The sudden wind shift, 6°C temperature drop and switch from falling to rising pressure all match the model's cold-front passage signature.

questions.prompt: Which development best fits this afternoon cloud record?
questions.context: Invented log, humid summer day. 11:00 small separate puffy clouds. 13:00 tall towers with flat, dark bases. 14:00 distant rumbling heard. Model rule: fast-growing towers with dark bases and thunder indicate showers developing nearby.

options.label: Showers or a thunderstorm developing nearby
A thin high veil replacing the clouds
Clouds dissolving into a clear sky

questions.explanation: Puffy clouds that grow into dark-based towers and produce thunder show strong rising air, so nearby showers fit best in this model.

questions.prompt: Order this clue-to-outcome chain from first step to last.
questions.context: Simplified model: sunlight heats the ground, warm air rises, rising air cools, vapor condenses into droplets, and showers fall from the cloud.
questions.explanation: Heating drives rising air; rising air cools; cooling lets vapor condense into droplets; once droplets grow large enough, they fall as showers.

questions.prompt: Using the logged times, order these observations from earliest to latest.
questions.context: Invented station notebook, listed unsorted: rain began 15:20; cloud base lowered 12:40; pressure fall first noted 06:10; thin high cloud thickened 09:30.
questions.explanation: Sorting the timestamps gives 06:10 pressure fall, 09:30 thickening cloud, 12:40 lower cloud base, then 15:20 rain.

questions.prompt: Match each clue set to the outcome it best supports in this model.
questions.context: Model labels: Drier fair spell needs rising pressure with falling humidity or clearing. Cold front just passed needs an abrupt wind shift with sharp cooling. Fog or dew needs air temperature reaching dew point.

left.label: Calm clear night, temperature falls to dew point
Wind jumps to northwest, 6°C drop in an hour
Steady pressure rise with falling humidity

questions.explanation: Rising pressure and drying air point to fair weather, cooling to dew point means condensation, falling pressure with lowering cloud means rain, and a sharp shift means a front.

questions.prompt: Which statement is best supported by this mixed evidence?
questions.context: Invented log. Pressure fell 2 hPa in three hours, but the gray layer broke into scattered puffy clouds and wind eased. Model rule: calling rain needs falling pressure plus thickening or lowering cloud.

options.label: Rain is not yet supported; check pressure and cloud again soon
Breaking clouds guarantee a dry day

questions.explanation: Only one rain clue is present and the cloud evidence disagrees, so the honest call is uncertainty. Another reading of pressure and cloud would settle it.

questions.prompt: For each situation, choose the single reading most useful to watch next.
questions.context: Model: cloud-top growth shows rising-air strength. The three-hour barometer trend shows approaching systems. The gap between temperature and dew point shows nearness to condensation. Wind and temperature after rain show air-mass change.

cells.label: Cumulus towers keep growing after noon

options.label: Cloud-top growth over the next hour
Wind and temperature after the showers

cells.label: Gray layer thickens; is a system approaching?

options.label: Cloud-top growth over the next hour
Wind and temperature after the showers

cells.label: Calm clear evening, air cooling toward dew point

options.label: Cloud-top growth over the next hour
Wind and temperature after the showers

cells.label: Warm humid showers just ended; air may change

options.label: Cloud-top growth over the next hour
Wind and temperature after the showers

questions.explanation: Each reading tests a different idea: tower growth for convection, barometer for approaching systems, dew-point gap for condensation, and wind shift for air-mass change.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data
USGS: water cycle

note: All logs, stations and readings are invented, and the rules are simplified teaching models. This is not a forecast tool and not safety guidance; check official weather services for real decisions.

title: Mystery Material
description: Solve eight reasoning puzzles that match what an object needs to the material property that explains it, then choose materials from a supplied property table.

questions.prompt: A kettle handle has four needs. Match each need to the property that explains it.
questions.context: Definitions: Low heat conduction means heat passes through slowly. Toughness means absorbing knocks without cracking. Moldability means it can be shaped while warm or liquid, then sets. Corrosion resistance means it does not rust or wear away from water and air.

cells.label: Stays comfortable to hold while the kettle body is hot
Survives being dropped on a tile floor without cracking
Can be pressed into a curved grip shape in a factory mold
Does not rust when splashed with water every day

questions.explanation: Each need points to one property: a cool grip depends on slow heat flow, drop survival on toughness, molded curves on moldability, and rust-free use on corrosion resistance.

questions.prompt: A model greenhouse panel must meet four needs. Match each need to the property behind it.
questions.context: Definitions: Transparency means light passes through. Stiffness means it resists bending. Low density means little weight for its size. Corrosion resistance means it does not rust or wear away from water and air.

cells.label: Lets sunlight reach the plants inside
Does not sag under its own weight when held at the edges
Is easy to carry because it weighs little for its size
Stays sound in constantly damp air

questions.explanation: Light passing through is transparency, holding shape is stiffness, carrying ease is low density, and lasting in damp air is corrosion resistance.

questions.prompt: A power-cord plug needs four things. Match each need to its explaining property.
questions.context: Definitions: Electrical insulation means current does not pass through. Flexibility means it bends repeatedly without snapping. Moldability means it can be shaped while warm or liquid, then sets. Stiffness means it resists bending.

cells.label: Keeps current away from the fingers holding the plug
The cord bends again and again at its entry point without snapping
Forms exact slots for metal pins when cast in a mold
The housing holds its shape instead of squashing when pressed

questions.explanation: Shielding fingers needs insulation, repeated bending needs flexibility, casting slots needs moldability, and resisting squashing needs stiffness.

questions.prompt: A kite faces four demands. Match each demand to the property that explains it.
questions.context: Definitions: Low density means little weight for its size. Stiffness means it resists bending. Flexibility means it bends without snapping. Toughness means absorbing knocks or snags without tearing or cracking.

cells.label: Wind can lift it because it weighs little for its size
The central spar stays straight under wind pressure
The line wraps around a reel without breaking
The sail does not rip when it snags on a branch

questions.explanation: Lift needs low density, a straight spar needs stiffness, reel winding needs flexibility, and surviving a snag needs toughness.

questions.prompt: Use the table to choose the one material whose properties meet each object's requirements.
questions.context: Invented table. Steel: conducts heat and electricity, stiff, tough, opaque, rusts. Glass: poor heat conductor, electrical insulator, stiff, brittle, transparent. Rubber: poor heat conductor, electrical insulator, very flexible, opaque. Hardwood: poor heat conductor, electrical insulator, stiff, opaque, rots if wet.

cells.label: Window on a storage box: must show contents and hold its shape
Jar-lid seal: must squeeze and spring back
Grounding rod: must be stiff and carry electric current

questions.explanation: Seeing through points to glass, springing back to rubber, and carrying current to steel; each is the only table entry with that property.

questions.prompt: Each object needs two properties together. Eliminate with the table and pick the one material that has both.
questions.context: Same invented table. Steel: conducts heat and electricity, stiff, tough, opaque. Glass: poor heat conductor, insulates electricity, stiff, transparent. Rubber: poor heat conductor, insulates electricity, very flexible, opaque. Hardwood: poor heat conductor, insulates electricity, stiff, opaque.

cells.label: Pan base: must be tough and move heat quickly
Lamp cover: must be see-through and a poor heat conductor
Cable sleeve: must bend repeatedly and block electric current
Tool handle: must be stiff, opaque and block electric current

questions.explanation: Two requirements remove rivals: fast heat plus toughness leaves steel, clear plus insulating leaves glass, bendy plus insulating leaves rubber, and stiff opaque insulating leaves hardwood.

questions.prompt: Match each everyday observation to the property it best demonstrates. Some properties are used more than once.
questions.context: Choose from Flexibility, Stiffness, Toughness and Low heat conduction, using the definitions from earlier puzzles.

left.label: A thin strip curls into a loop and springs straight again
A rod held at one end barely sags
A tile dropped on the floor only picks up a dent
A mug wall stays touchable while the drink inside is hot
A beam under a heavy load hardly bends

questions.explanation: Springing back is flexibility, resisting sag or bending is stiffness, absorbing a drop is toughness, and a cool outer wall reflects slow heat flow.

questions.prompt: Mystery Material M is opaque, flexible, a poor heat conductor, and blocks electric current. Which job needs only properties M has?
questions.context: Invented case. Material M: opaque, flexible, poor heat conductor, electrical insulator. It is not transparent, not stiff, and does not carry current.

options.label: A display panel that must be see-through
A soft pot-lid knob that must stay cool when the pot is hot
A wire core that must carry current
A rigid shelf bracket that must not bend

questions.explanation: A cool, soft knob needs slow heat flow and flexibility, which M has. The other jobs need transparency, current-carrying, or stiffness, which M lacks.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All materials, tables and objects here are simplified invented cases. Every property you need is given in the puzzle, so no outside knowledge or experiments are required.

title: Build a Food Web
description: Wire up who eats whom in three simplified habitat models, then follow the rules to trace what changes when one species is removed.

sections.title: Wire the habitats
sections.description: Link each consumer to its food source.

sections.title: Remove a species
sections.description: Apply the model rules to predict effects.

sections.title: Trace the ripples
sections.description: Order and sort effects by how far they travel.

questions.prompt: Match each pond animal to the one thing it eats in this invented pond web.
questions.explanation: Tadpoles and mayfly nymphs share algae as food. The remaining grazer is the tadpole, so dragonfly nymphs eat tadpoles, and herons eat the dragonfly nymphs.
questions.context: Invented model. Clues: Tadpoles eat the pond's only producer. Mayfly nymphs eat the same food as tadpoles. Dragonfly nymphs hunt the grazer that is not a mayfly nymph. Herons eat only the hunter.

questions.prompt: Link each meadow animal to its single food source in this invented grassland web.
questions.explanation: Grass feeds both plant eaters. Meadowlarks take the insect, while hawks and coyotes both rely on the burrowing mammal, so two predators share one target.
questions.context: Invented model. Clues: Grasshoppers eat the meadow's only plant, grass. Voles eat the same food as grasshoppers. Meadowlarks eat only insects. Hawks and coyotes both eat only the burrowing mammal.

questions.prompt: Wire this simplified kelp forest: match each animal to the single food it eats.
questions.explanation: Urchins and snails both graze kelp. Otters take the spiny grazer, the urchin, and rockfish take the grazer without spines, the snail.
questions.context: Invented model. Clues: Urchins and snails both graze the only producer, kelp. Sea otters eat only the spiny grazer. Rockfish eat only the grazer without spines.

questions.prompt: All minnows are removed. For each feeding link, decide whether it disappears or stays.
questions.explanation: A link needs both species. Only links where minnows eat or are eaten vanish. The snail and dragonfly links involve other species, so they remain.
questions.context: Invented pond web. Snails eat algae. Minnows eat snails. Kingfishers eat only minnows. Dragonfly larvae eat snails.

cells.label: Snails eat algae
Minnows eat snails
Kingfishers eat minnows
Dragonfly larvae eat snails

questions.prompt: Sea otters are removed from the kelp forest. Apply the rules to each species.
questions.explanation: Urchins rise first, so kelp falls. Snails then lose their only food and fall, and rockfish follow. These are outcomes of the stated rules, not real forecasts.
questions.context: Web: kelp is eaten by urchins and snails. Otters eat only urchins. Rockfish eat only snails. Rules, applied in rounds: 1) Prey of a removed species rises. 2) Food eaten by a rising species falls. 3) A species whose only food falls, falls. A species keeps the first change it gets.

cells.label: Urchins
Kelp
Snails
Rockfish

questions.prompt: Mayfly nymphs vanish from this invented mountain stream. Apply the rules to decide each species' change.
questions.explanation: Dippers lose their only food and fall. Trout keep caddis larvae as food, so they stay the same. Algae loses one of two grazer groups and rises. Caddis larvae are not reached by rules 1 to 3, so rule 4 keeps them the same.
questions.context: Web: algae is eaten by mayfly nymphs and caddis larvae. Trout eat both mayfly nymphs and caddis larvae. Dippers eat only mayfly nymphs. Rules: 1) A predator with another food source stays the same. 2) A predator with no other food falls. 3) Food that loses one of its two consumer groups rises. 4) Any species not changed by rules 1 to 3 stays the same.

cells.label: Trout
Dippers
Algae
Caddis larvae

questions.prompt: Snails are removed from the pond. Order the ripple steps so every cause comes before its effect.
questions.explanation: Snail loss both frees algae from grazing and cuts the minnows' only food. Kingfishers can only fall after minnows do, but the algae step is independent of that chain.
questions.context: Invented pond web. Snails eat algae. Minnows eat only snails. Kingfishers eat only minnows. Rules: algae eaten by fewer grazers rises; a species whose only food falls, falls.

questions.prompt: Minnows are removed. Sort each species by how many links away it is from the minnows.
questions.explanation: Kingfishers and snails touch minnows directly. Algae and dragonfly larvae link to snails, so they are second ripples. Frogs link only to dragonfly larvae, which puts them three links away.
questions.context: Invented pond web. Snails eat algae. Minnows eat snails. Kingfishers eat only minnows. Dragonfly larvae eat snails. Frogs eat only dragonfly larvae. First ripple: directly linked to minnows. Second ripple: directly linked to a first-ripple species.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: Every habitat here is a simplified, invented model with all rules supplied. Results show what the stated rules produce, not forecasts for real ecosystems.

title: Where Was the Light?
description: Eight shadow puzzles on level ground: read shadow direction and length from supplied diagrams and data to locate a distant light and how high it sits.

questions.prompt: Tap the part of the sky where the single distant light must be.
questions.context: Top-down schematic: north is up, east is right. A tall post stands at the centre on level ground. Its shadow stretches across the ground toward the east edge.
questions.explanation: A shadow points directly away from the light. Since the shadow runs east, the light is on the opposite side, in the west.

diagram.title: Post and eastward shadow, top-down
diagram.description: A top-down square map with north up. A post sits at the centre and its shadow extends to the right (east). Four labelled zones sit at the north, east, south and west edges.

questions.prompt: Tap the corner of the sky where the light must be.
questions.context: Top-down schematic: north is up, east is right. A post stands at the centre of level ground, and its shadow runs diagonally toward the bottom-left corner, which is southwest.
questions.explanation: The light lies opposite the shadow. A shadow pointing southwest means the light is in the northeast, the top-right corner.

diagram.title: Post and diagonal shadow, top-down
diagram.description: A top-down square map with north up. A post at the centre casts a shadow toward the bottom-left. Four corner zones are labelled by compass direction.

questions.prompt: Which compass direction is the light in?
questions.context: A printed map is turned so that north points to the right edge of the page. Two equal posts both cast shadows pointing to the top edge of the page.
questions.explanation: With north on the right, the top of the page is west. Shadows point west, so the light is on the opposite side, in the east.

questions.prompt: Using the measurements, which direction is the light in?
questions.context: On a grid with x pointing east and y pointing north, a post's base is at (0, 0). The tip of its shadow lands at (-3, +3) metres.
questions.explanation: The tip is 3 m west and 3 m north of the base, so the shadow points northwest. The light is opposite, in the southeast.

questions.prompt: Match each shadow observation to the direction of the light.
questions.context: Compass directions are standard, with north up. Several observations can point to the same light direction.
questions.explanation: Each light sits opposite its shadow. The tip 4 m east and 4 m north of the base is a northeast shadow, so it shares the southwest light.

left.label: Shadow tip is 4 m east and 4 m north of the base

questions.prompt: What happened to the light's height above the horizon?
questions.context: A 2 m post on level ground first casts a 2 m shadow. Later, with the same post, its shadow measures 4 m.
questions.explanation: A longer shadow from the same post means the light is shallower. The first angle is 45 degrees; the second is smaller, so the light dropped lower.

options.label: The light stayed at the same height
The post must have grown taller

questions.prompt: Which description matches how the light changed?
questions.context: The same 3 m post first casts a 5 m shadow pointing north. Later its shadow is 2 m long and points northeast.
questions.explanation: The shadow shortened, so the light climbed higher. The shadow turned from north to northeast, so the light moved from south toward southwest.

options.label: Higher, moving from south toward southwest
Lower, moving from south toward southwest
Higher, moving from north toward northeast
Lower, moving from north toward northeast

questions.prompt: Order these light heights from the shortest shadow to the longest shadow.
questions.context: One post of fixed height is lit by a distant light at four heights above the horizon: 20 degrees, 45 degrees, 60 degrees and 70 degrees. The same post is used each time.
questions.explanation: The higher the light, the shorter the shadow. Shadow length shrinks as elevation rises, so 70 degrees is shortest and 20 degrees is longest.

title: The Sound You Cannot See
description: Across eight tasks, listen to original tone clips and solve text puzzles to work out what a sound traveled through, which path change altered it, and how far an echo went.

sections.title: Name the path
sections.description: Use each clip's legend to identify the medium or source.

sections.title: Compare and explain
sections.description: Work out which change happened and why.

questions.prompt: Using the legend, which path produced this clip?
questions.context: Legend for this puzzle. Open air: 800 Hz and 300 Hz together. Thick wall: only 300 Hz. Metal pipe: 800 Hz in three quick pulses. Distant echo: 300 Hz twice, 0.5 seconds apart.
questions.transcript: One steady low tone at 300 Hz lasting 0.4 seconds. No high 800 Hz tone and no repeat.
questions.explanation: Only the low 300 Hz component is present, which the legend assigns to the thick wall. Open air would also include the 800 Hz tone.

questions.prompt: Using the pulse-count legend, what made this sound?
questions.context: Legend: each source plays 400 Hz pulses. One pulse is a dropped book. Two pulses is a door knock. Three pulses is footsteps. Four pulses is a machine tick.
questions.transcript: Three short 400 Hz pulses, each 0.1 seconds long, starting at 0, 0.35 and 0.7 seconds.
questions.explanation: Counting pulses is the whole key: three evenly spaced pulses match the footsteps code. The pitch is the same for every source, so it cannot decide.

questions.prompt: Which of the two paths delivered the sound faster in this clip?
questions.context: Legend: one clap reaches a sensor along two paths. The 600 Hz tone marks arrival through air. The 900 Hz tone marks arrival through water. The tone heard first came by the faster path.
questions.transcript: A 900 Hz tone at 0 seconds, then a 600 Hz tone at 0.8 seconds, each 0.2 seconds long.

options.label: The legend gives no way to tell

questions.explanation: The 900 Hz water-path tone arrives first, 0.8 seconds before the air-path tone. Whichever arrival comes first took the faster path.

questions.prompt: In this model, a recording has 200 Hz and 1000 Hz parts. Behind the wall, a listener hears only 200 Hz. What was blocked?
questions.context: Model rule: a wall path lets low tones through but blocks high tones. Open air passes both. This is a simplified teaching model, not a measurement.
questions.explanation: The wall passes the low 200 Hz tone and removes the high 1000 Hz tone, which is why the sound loses its sharp edge and seems muffled.

questions.prompt: Match each recording change to the path change that explains it.
questions.context: Model rules: a barrier removes high tones. A reflecting surface adds a delayed copy of the sound. A longer path keeps every tone but makes it quieter.

left.label: The 1000 Hz tone vanished; 200 Hz remains
The same thump repeats 0.6 seconds later
All tones are intact but gain fell from 0.10 to 0.05
After a hallway door closed, 900 Hz disappeared

questions.explanation: Lost high tones signal a barrier, including the closed door. A delayed identical copy signals a reflection, and uniformly quieter tones signal a longer path.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order a drum thump travels to a neighbor's room.
questions.context: Simplified model: each step directly causes the next one, passing the vibration along a single chain.

items.label: Air in the practice room vibrates
Air in the neighbor's room vibrates

questions.explanation: The vibration starts at the drum, moves through the room's air into the wall, then passes through the wall into the neighbor's air.

questions.prompt: For each clip pair, choose the change that explains how clip B differs from clip A.
questions.context: Model rules: a barrier removes 900 Hz but keeps 300 Hz. A longer path lowers gain but keeps every tone. A reflecting surface adds a delayed copy. A source pitch change shifts the tone frequencies.

cells.label: Pair 1: A has 900 Hz and 300 Hz; B has only 300 Hz
Pair 2: A has gain 0.10; B has the same tones at gain 0.05
Pair 3: A is one thump; B is that thump plus a copy 0.6 seconds later

questions.explanation: Each difference matches exactly one rule: missing highs mean a barrier, uniform quieting means a longer path, and a delayed copy means a reflection.

questions.prompt: A clap and its echo are heard as below. How far away is the reflecting wall?
questions.context: Assume sound travels 340 meters per second in this problem. The first tone is the clap, the second is the echo, which traveled to the wall and back.
questions.transcript: Two identical 600 Hz pulses, each 0.1 seconds long, the first at 0 seconds and the second at 0.5 seconds.
questions.explanation: In 0.5 seconds the sound covers 170 meters, but that is a round trip to the wall and back, so the wall is half that: 85 meters.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All clips are original synthetic tones, and each puzzle supplies its own simplified legend, so the answers come from the rules shown. Every audio task has a text transcript for a no-audio route. This is not a hearing test.

title: The Pollinator Shift
description: Guide an invented garden through spring, summer and autumn. Solve bloom-timing puzzles for an accuracy score, then see two separate preference scales: Quick Tweaker to Slow Observer and Focused Planter to Mixed Planter. Taste choices have no correct answer.

sections.title: Spring
sections.description: Early blooms and the bees that follow.

sections.title: Summer
sections.description: Keeping flowers open while pollinators forage.

sections.title: Autumn
sections.description: One late-season task, depending on your spring choice.

dimensions.description: Whether you tend to act on a garden problem right away or watch and gather notes first.
Whether you lean toward a few reliable plants or many different flower types.

questions.prompt: Which single addition would give the bees food when they emerge on day 15?
questions.context: Invented garden: Snowbell flowers bloom days 3–11. Mason bees emerge on day 15 and forage until day 60. No other flower in the bed opens before day 30.
questions.explanation: The gap runs from day 12 to day 29. Only a flower open on day 15 helps; staggering bloom windows covers it.

options.label: A second flower that also blooms days 3–11
Nothing; Snowbell alone will carry them

questions.prompt: Order these spring plants by the day their bloom ends, earliest first.
questions.context: Invented bloom windows: Snowbell days 3–11. Lungwort days 8–40. Columbine days 22–30. Catmint days 28–52.
questions.explanation: End days are Snowbell 11, Columbine 30, Lungwort 40, Catmint 52. Start days alone would give a different order.

questions.prompt: An empty corner is left in the spring bed. How do you handle it?
questions.explanation: This is a style choice with no right answer. It sets which short autumn task you see next.

options.label: Watch the corner all spring and note which visitors arrive
Fill it now with a mix of several flower types

questions.prompt: Midsummer, your bed looks quiet. What do you do first?
questions.explanation: There is no correct answer here. Each response shows a different gardening habit, scored only for your garden summary.

options.label: Keep a daily log for a week before changing anything
Add a new flower type to draw a different visitor
Stay with your current plants and wait for the next bloom
Trim and replace the fading plants right away

questions.prompt: Bees forage days 60–100. On which days is no flower open?
questions.context: Invented summer bed. Bergamot blooms days 60–72. Coneflower blooms days 70–85. Rudbeckia blooms days 90–100.
questions.explanation: Coneflower ends on day 85 and Rudbeckia starts on day 90, leaving days 86–89 bare. The other windows are covered.

questions.prompt: Match each summer situation with the response you would likely choose.
questions.explanation: These are unkeyed preferences. Many situations can share one response, and your pattern feeds only the garden summary.

left.label: A lull with few blooms for five days
A new patch has no visitors yet
One flower type dominates the bed

right.label: Wait a week and keep notes
Keep the bed as it is

questions.prompt: Which one new plant would close the gap in bee food?
questions.context: Invented autumn bed. Bees are active weeks 1–8. Aster blooms weeks 1–4. Goldenrod blooms weeks 3–5. Sedum blooms weeks 7–8.
questions.explanation: Week 6 has no open flower. Only late mint, blooming weeks 5–6, covers it. The other windows overlap existing blooms or miss the gap.

questions.prompt: Which addition would bring in a visitor type your bed does not yet serve?
questions.context: Invented rules: mason bees visit only tube-shaped flowers, hoverflies visit only flat flowers. Both are active weeks 1–6. Your bed has only flat flowers.
questions.explanation: Hoverflies are already served by flat flowers. Only a tube flower open during weeks 1–6 adds mason bees, so the week 2–6 tube flower works.

note: All gardens, plants, dates and bee rules are invented for these puzzles and are not real horticultural advice. Your knowledge score and garden-style summary are kept separate, and taste choices are never marked right or wrong.

title: Cause Chain Courtroom
description: Judge short cause-and-effect chains: match each link to its mechanism or evidence, then find the link where the argument is weakest.

sections.title: Link the Mechanisms
sections.description: Match links to mechanisms and evidence.

sections.title: Find the Weak Link
sections.description: Judge supplied evidence and spot the gap.

questions.prompt: Match each link in the litter-and-soil story to the mechanism that supports it.
questions.context: Simplified model: decomposers are organisms that feed on dead leaves. Mechanisms: food supply, nutrient release, surface cover, or heat release. Choose one for each link.

cells.label: More leaf litter → more decomposer feeding

options.label: Food supply: more material to eat
Surface cover shields soil from sun and wind

cells.label: More decomposer feeding → more nutrients in soil

options.label: Food supply: more material to eat
Surface cover shields soil from sun and wind

cells.label: Thicker litter layer → slower soil drying

options.label: Food supply: more material to eat
Surface cover shields soil from sun and wind

questions.explanation: Each link needs its own mechanism: feeding needs food, nutrients come from broken-down tissue, and a covering layer slows drying at the surface.

questions.prompt: Match each link in this rainstorm chain to the process that explains it.
questions.context: Infiltration is water entering the ground. Runoff is water flowing across the surface. Chain: compacted soil, less infiltration, more runoff, more soil carried away.

cells.label: Compacted soil → less infiltration

options.label: Squeezed pores leave fewer openings for water to enter

cells.label: Less infiltration → more runoff

options.label: Water that cannot enter the ground has more left to flow over it
Ground water turns into rain instantly
Condensation pulls water into the soil
Roots lift surface water into clouds

cells.label: More runoff → more soil carried away

options.label: Water vapor compresses the soil in place
Flowing water can lift and carry loose particles

questions.explanation: Compaction reduces openings, unabsorbed water stays on the surface, and moving surface water can carry particles with it.

questions.prompt: Match each link in the invented pond chain to the evidence card that directly tests it.
questions.context: Invented pond study. Chain: warm days → more algae → lower night oxygen → fish near the surface.

left.label: Low oxygen → fish near the surface

right.label: Morning fish counts on low-oxygen days
Daily temperature log beside algae counts
Night sensor readings beside algae counts

questions.explanation: Each link needs evidence measuring both of its ends. Rainfall totals measure neither end of any link here.

questions.prompt: Sort each invented study by whether it is a controlled comparison or an observed pattern only.
questions.context: A controlled comparison means researchers set up the difference themselves and compare similar groups.

left.label: Leaf bags with microbes and matching sterile bags were weighed after 60 days.
Forest plots with deeper litter had richer soil; nobody chose which plots got litter.
Researchers added litter to 6 randomly chosen plots and left 6 similar plots bare.
Gardeners say plots near big trees look greener.

questions.explanation: Setting up the difference yourself with similar comparison groups tests cause more strongly. Noticing that two things go together does not.

questions.prompt: Judge each link of the parking-lot chain using only the data supplied.
questions.context: Invented data. Chain: new parking lot → more runoff → higher stream peaks → fewer insect larvae. Gauge: runoff after storms rose after paving. No stream-height readings exist. Larvae fell, but a chemical spill upstream happened the same month.

cells.label: Parking lot → more runoff
More runoff → higher stream peaks
Higher peaks → fewer larvae

questions.explanation: A link can be measured, unmeasured, or confounded. The spill offers a rival cause for the larvae drop, and stream peaks were never recorded.

questions.prompt: Judge each link of the shade-tree chain using only the data supplied.
questions.context: Invented data. Chain: shade trees → cooler soil → slower leaf decay → thicker litter. Shaded plots were 3°C cooler. Leaf bags lost equal mass in shaded and sunny plots over 60 days. Shaded plots had thicker litter but also received more falling leaves.

cells.label: Shade trees → cooler soil
Cooler soil → slower leaf decay
Slower decay → thicker litter

questions.explanation: Equal mass loss contradicts slower decay. Thicker litter has a rival explanation, since shaded plots also received more leaves.

questions.prompt: Each chain has three links rated for evidence. Assign each chain to its weakest link.
questions.context: Invented ratings, given as links 1, 2, 3 in order. Scale: 3 = lab-tested, 2 = field-measured, 1 = anecdote only. The weakest link has the lowest rating. Each chain has exactly one lowest link.
questions.explanation: Read each chain's lowest rating. Two chains share Link 3 as their weakest point, so several chains can point to the same link.

questions.prompt: Which link most needs stronger evidence before this chain is trusted?
questions.context: Invented chain: more leaf litter → more decomposer feeding → more soil nutrients → taller seedlings. Links 1 to 3 were each measured in field plots. Link 4 rests only on gardeners' memories, with no measurements.

options.label: Link 1, because litter is easy to see
Link 2, because feeding is a biological process
Link 4, because only memories support it

questions.explanation: A chain is only as convincing as its least-supported step. Measured links outweigh recollection, so the seedling-height link is the gap.

title: Field Notebook Style
description: Choose, match, slide and rank your way through eight nature-notebook scenes, then see two preference scales: Details to Patterns and Sketching to Counting. There is no correct answer.

sections.title: Observation moments
sections.description: Pick what you would record first.

sections.title: Your notebook page
sections.description: Arrange how you would fill a page.

dimensions.description: Whether you tend to note one close feature first or how things repeat and relate across a scene.
Whether you tend to capture a scene with drawn shapes or with tallies, numbers and measurements.

questions.prompt: On a woodland path you can record one thing first. Which do you note?
questions.explanation: There is no right answer. Close textures lean toward details; repeating calls lean toward patterns.

options.label: The texture of one leaf's surface
The repeating rhythm of a birdsong
A quick outline of one feather you spot
How many different bird calls you hear in a minute

questions.prompt: You stop at a small pond. What goes in your notebook first?
questions.explanation: Drawing and counting are both valid ways to start. This question mostly separates sketching from counting.

options.label: A sketch of the ripples and reflections
A count of lily pads in view
Tally marks of dragonflies passing each minute
A drawing of one lily pad's veins

questions.prompt: In a sunny meadow, which observation do you write down first?
questions.explanation: Zooming in on a single flower is a detail habit; noticing clusters or spacing is a pattern habit.

options.label: The markings on one flower's petals
How flower colors cluster in patches
The posture of one small insect's legs

questions.prompt: You reach a pebbly shoreline. What do you record first?
questions.explanation: Each choice is a legitimate way to begin a page. Your picks only show your leaning today.

options.label: A sketch of the curving line where waves reach
A tally of shells sorted by type
Marks showing how far the tide line sits at set times
A drawing of one shell's spiral

questions.prompt: Match each thing you notice to the note style you would use for it.
questions.explanation: Several observations can share one style. Your assignments show which note styles you reach for most.

left.label: A flock of birds crossing the sky

questions.prompt: Where does your ideal notebook page sit between drawings and numbers?
questions.explanation: Neither end is better. A page of drawings and a page of counts both preserve what you saw.

questions.prompt: Rank what you would give most space on a page, from most to least.
questions.explanation: Your order reflects taste, not skill. Close detail and repeating pattern pull opposite ways on the first axis.

questions.prompt: Rank these page extras by how much you would want them, most to least.
questions.explanation: Each extra suits a different note style. Your ranking shows a leaning, not a better or worse notebook.

items.label: A magnified drawing of one feature
A tally table of repeated sightings
A rough layout sketch of where things sit
An exact measurement of one item

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: This is a playful preference activity with invented scenes. No notebook style is better than another, and results are not a personality or ability measure.

title: Tiny Terrarium Logic
description: Assign roles to the parts of a paper-model sealed jar, then follow stated rules through three-step changes to see which effects the model supports and which it leaves open.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the paper-model jar to the role it plays in the model.
questions.context: Model roles: an energy source supplies light. A producer is a plant that uses light to grow. A condensation surface is a cool surface where vapor turns into liquid droplets.
questions.explanation: Lamp light feeds growth, both moss and fern are producers, and the cool glass is where vapor condenses. Two parts can share one role.

questions.prompt: Match each water movement in the model jar to its process name.
questions.context: Use simplified definitions: liquid becoming gas, gas becoming liquid, water entering the ground, and water flowing over a surface.
questions.explanation: Evaporation is liquid to gas, condensation is gas to liquid, infiltration is water entering the ground, and runoff is water flowing over the surface.

left.label: Liquid on damp soil becomes vapor
Vapor becomes beads on cool glass
Water soaks down into the soil
Water flows downhill across the soil surface

questions.prompt: Assign each model variable to the loop it belongs to.
questions.context: Energy loop: variables about light input. Water loop: variables that hold or move water. Nutrient loop: variables that hold or move decay products. Each variable belongs to exactly one loop.
questions.explanation: Lamp brightness is light input. Fog and damp soil hold or move water. Decaying leaves and released nutrients handle decay products.

questions.prompt: Lamp light is reduced in the model. Predict each effect, using only the rules given.
questions.context: Rules: lower light lowers plant growth. Lower plant growth lowers leaf drop. Lower leaf drop lowers food for decomposers. No rule links light to soil dampness.
questions.explanation: Three rules chain downward from light to decomposer food. Soil dampness has no rule connecting it to this change, so the model does not specify it.

cells.label: Plant growth
Leaf drop
Food for decomposers
Soil dampness

questions.prompt: In the model, leaf drop is set to zero. Predict each downstream effect.
questions.context: Rules: lower leaf drop lowers decomposer food. Lower decomposer food lowers nutrient release. Lower nutrient release lowers plant growth. Lower plant growth raises light reaching the soil.
questions.explanation: Each rule passes the decrease along, ending in lower growth. The last rule flips direction, so more light reaches the soil.

cells.label: Decomposer food
Nutrient release
Plant growth
Light reaching the soil

questions.prompt: Plant growth rises in the model. Decide which effects follow, and which cannot be decided.
questions.context: Rules: more growth raises leaf drop. More leaf drop raises decomposer food. More growth lowers light reaching soil. More growth lowers soil dampness by drawing water. More leaf drop raises soil dampness. No rule gives the strengths.
questions.explanation: The first three effects follow from single rules. Soil dampness gets two opposing rules with no strengths, so the net direction cannot be decided.

cells.label: Leaf drop
Food for decomposers
Light reaching the soil
Soil dampness

questions.prompt: A player says this model proves a sealed jar stays balanced for years. What does the model actually support?
questions.context: The model lists only directions of change, such as lower light lowers plant growth. It gives no amounts, no time spans and no real-jar measurements.
questions.explanation: Direction-only rules support qualitative what-if reasoning. Without amounts or time spans, they cannot show how long any real jar lasts.

options.label: Jars stay balanced for a fixed number of years
Only the stated directions of linked changes, with no amounts or durations
Exact moisture levels for any jar
Which plants to buy for a real jar

questions.prompt: Order the model events so that every cause comes before its effect.
questions.context: Rules: the lamp warms the soil before water evaporates. Water evaporates before vapor condenses. Vapor condenses before droplets return to soil. The moss grows only after the lamp lights it. Moss growth is independent of the water events.
questions.explanation: The water events form a strict chain after the lamp. Moss growth only needs the lamp first, so it can fit anywhere after that step.

items.label: Lamp warms and lights the jar
Moss uses the light to grow

USGS: water cycle

note: The jar, its rules and all cause-and-effect links are an invented paper model. This is a digital reasoning exercise only, with no building instructions and no claims about real terrariums.

title: Where Did the Energy Go
description: Put four everyday energy transfers in order, then pick the right account of where energy ended up in four short scenarios.

sections.title: Follow the chain
sections.description: Order the steps of each energy transfer.

sections.title: Account for it
sections.description: Decide where the energy went.

questions.prompt: A pendulum bob is released from a raised position and swings across. Order the energy steps from first to last.
questions.context: Ignore air resistance and friction for this simplified swing. The steps are listed in mixed order.

items.label: The bob rises on the far side as motion energy turns back into height energy
The bob is held still at its highest point with maximum stored height energy
The bob passes its lowest point at top speed
The bob is released and speeds up as it falls

questions.explanation: Stored height energy becomes motion energy on the way down, peaking at the lowest point, then converts back to height energy as the bob climbs.

questions.prompt: Follow the energy from an unlit log to a hand warming beside a campfire. What is the order?
questions.context: Treat the fire as a simple chain: stored energy, release, spread, then arrival. Steps are shown in mixed order.

items.label: A nearby hand warms up as thermal energy arrives
Burning releases the stored energy as heat and light
The unlit log holds stored chemical energy
Heat and light spread outward into the surrounding air

questions.explanation: Fuel stores chemical energy, burning releases it as heat and light, and that energy spreads outward until something nearby, like a hand, absorbs it.

questions.prompt: A hand-crank flashlight lights up when someone turns the crank. Put the energy transfers in order.
questions.context: Assume the crank turns a small generator that powers the bulb directly. Steps are shown in mixed order.

items.label: The bulb turns electrical energy into light, plus some heat
The generator turns motion energy into electrical energy
The person's muscles use stored chemical energy from food
The muscles turn the crank, giving it motion energy

questions.explanation: Chemical energy in muscles becomes crank motion, the generator converts that motion to electrical energy, and the bulb converts it to light and some heat.

questions.prompt: A solar garden lamp charges by day and shines at night. Order the steps; one step can happen at any point after sunlight arrives.
questions.context: Model: sunlight reaches the panel, the panel makes electrical energy, the battery stores it, and later the lamp uses it. The panel also warms slightly once sunlight hits it.

items.label: The battery stores the energy chemically
The panel warms slightly in the sun
At night the lamp turns stored energy into light
The panel turns some of the light into electrical energy

questions.explanation: The main chain runs sunlight, electrical energy, battery storage, then lamp light. Panel warming only needs to follow sunlight, so it can fit anywhere after that.

questions.prompt: A ball rolls across a flat floor and slowly stops. Which account of its motion energy is best?
questions.context: Model rule: energy is not destroyed; it changes form or spreads into surroundings.

options.label: It disappears once the ball stops moving
Friction spreads it as slight warming of the ball and floor, plus tiny sound and air motion
It is stored in the ball as extra height energy
It is converted into light given off by the ball

questions.explanation: Friction and air drag transfer the ball's motion energy to its surroundings as tiny amounts of heat, sound and air movement. The total energy is conserved.

questions.prompt: A phone with a dark screen charges overnight, and the charger feels slightly warm. Where does the electrical energy go?
questions.context: Simplified phone-and-charger model: the phone is off and no light or sound is produced. Of every 10 energy units entering the charger, 9 are stored in the phone's battery and 1 leaves the charger as heat.

options.label: All of it is stored in the battery
Most is stored in the battery, with the remainder leaving as heat
All of it becomes light from the screen
It vanishes once the battery is full

questions.explanation: In this model, 9 of every 10 units are stored chemically and 1 leaves as heat, which is why the charger feels warm. Nothing simply vanishes.

questions.prompt: An ice cube melts in a glass of warm lemonade, and the drink cools. What explains the energy flow?
questions.context: Treat the glass as a closed system for this question.

options.label: Cold energy flows from the ice into the drink
Thermal energy flows from the warmer drink into the ice, melting it and cooling the drink
The ice gives thermal energy to the drink, which warms it up
Thermal energy disappears as the ice melts

questions.explanation: Thermal energy moves from the warmer drink to the colder ice. The ice melts using that energy, while the drink loses it and cools.

questions.prompt: An old filament bulb takes in 40 energy units each second, and 36 units leave as heat. How many leave as light?
questions.context: In this invented model the bulb has only two outputs, heat and light, and no energy is stored in the bulb.
questions.explanation: Energy in equals energy out. With 40 units in and 36 leaving as heat, the remaining 4 units must leave as light.

note: The scenarios are simplified models with every rule and number given in the question. They ignore small real-world effects unless noted.

title: Fair Test Designer
description: Design simple plant, ramp and dissolving experiments by choosing what to change, keep the same and measure, then spot flaws in other people's tests.

sections.title: Keep it fair
sections.description: Choose the right controls and measurements.

sections.title: Roles and steps
sections.description: Sort variables and plan a test.

sections.title: Find the flaw
sections.description: Spot what weakens a test.

questions.prompt: You compare two seedlings, changing only how much light each gets. What must stay the same?
questions.context: Both seedlings are the same type and start at the same size.
questions.explanation: Only the tested factor, light, should differ. Water, soil and temperature must match so they cannot explain any growth difference.

options.label: Water amount, soil type and temperature
The amount of light each seedling gets
The final height of each seedling
The seedling that is placed first on the shelf

questions.prompt: You test whether a cloth or smooth card ramp surface changes how far a toy car rolls. What stays the same?
questions.explanation: Ramp height, the same car and a hands-off release keep the surface as the only difference. Changing the car or pushing would add other causes.

options.label: Ramp height, the same car and a release without pushing
A heavy car on cloth and a light car on card
A higher ramp for the card surface

questions.prompt: You ask whether a steeper ramp makes a car reach the bottom sooner. Which measurement answers that question?
questions.context: Every run uses the same car, the same 1 metre track, and a release without pushing.
questions.explanation: Time to travel the fixed track directly measures how soon the car arrives. Colour or sound do not measure arrival time.

options.label: The colour of the car after each run
The time to travel the same 1 metre track

questions.prompt: You compare bean growth in bright light and dim light. Which plan makes the result more trustworthy?
questions.explanation: Several seedlings per condition, averaged, reduce the chance that one unusual plant misleads you. A single hand-picked plant can hide natural variation.

options.label: Use five seedlings per light condition and compare the averages
Use one seedling per condition, choosing the tallest for bright light
Pick the healthiest-looking seedling for the bright group

questions.prompt: Match each item to its role in a test of whether stirring changes how fast salt dissolves.
questions.context: Identical cups each hold the same water and salt. One is stirred, one is not, and you time how long until no grains are visible.
questions.explanation: Stirring is the one thing changed, time is what you measure, and the water and salt amounts are held constant for fairness.

left.label: Time until no grains are visible
Amount of water in each cup
Amount of salt in each cup

questions.prompt: Put these fair-test planning steps in a sensible order.
questions.explanation: You need a question first, then one change, then the controls, then the trials, then the records, and finally the comparison.

items.label: Choose the one thing to change
Decide what to keep the same
Run every trial and record results

questions.prompt: Mia puts one seedling on a sunny sill in a large pot of rich soil, and another in a dark cupboard in a small pot of ordinary soil. What is the flaw?
questions.explanation: Pot size and soil differ along with light, so a growth difference could come from any of them. Only light should differ.

options.label: Pot size and soil also differ, so light is not isolated
She measured in centimetres instead of inches
She should have used different plant species

questions.prompt: Choose the main flaw in each of these three test designs.
questions.context: Design A: a ramp is steep for one car and shallow for another, and the steep-ramp car is pushed. Design B: sunny seedlings are measured after 5 days, shaded ones after 10 days. Design C: cloth and card ramp surfaces each get one run, and the results are compared.
questions.explanation: A pushed car has an extra force, unequal measuring times give unequal growth time, and a single run per surface cannot show whether the result repeats.

cells.label: Design A: steep ramp car is pushed
Design B: measured after 5 and 10 days
Design C: one run per surface

title: Rock Cycle Road Trip
description: Follow one imaginary rock through heat, weather and pressure. Pick the change each stated condition supports, choose a route, then trace the resulting material.

sections.title: Three Forks
sections.description: Pick the change the stated conditions support.

sections.title: Trace the Consequences
sections.description: Follow the rock down the road you choose.

questions.prompt: A sandstone is buried deep at 400°C under high pressure. Which change do the field-card rules support?
questions.context: Field card (simplified game model): a solid rock that is hot and squeezed, but below its melting point, recrystallizes into metamorphic rock. Above its melting point it becomes magma. Rock at the surface weathers. This sandstone's melting point is 900°C.
questions.explanation: At 400°C the rock is far below 900°C, so it stays solid. Deep heat and pressure change its minerals into metamorphic rock instead.

options.label: It becomes metamorphic rock while staying solid
It breaks into loose sediment at the surface

questions.prompt: Your road bends past a magma chamber. A marble-like rock heats to 1,150°C. What happens next?
questions.context: Field card (simplified game model): a rock heated above its melting point turns to magma. This rock's melting point is 1,000°C. Pressure stays high, but melting depends here only on the stated melting point.
questions.explanation: 1,150°C is above the 1,000°C melting point given on the card, so the rock melts into magma rather than staying solid.

questions.prompt: A cliff rock sits in open air at 12°C, hit by rain and frost, with no deep burial. What is supported?
questions.context: Field card (simplified game model): rain, frost and wind break exposed rock into fragments, called weathering. Melting needs temperatures above 900°C here, and metamorphism needs deep heat and pressure.
questions.explanation: The cliff is cool, exposed and not buried, so neither melting nor metamorphism applies. Weathering breaks it into fragments.

options.label: It is already cemented sedimentary rock

questions.prompt: Match each stop on the road to the rock class it produces.
questions.context: Reference diagram (simplified): cooled magma or lava gives igneous rock. Sediment that is compacted and cemented gives sedimentary rock. Solid rock changed by heat and pressure without melting gives metamorphic rock.
questions.explanation: The process decides the class: cooling melt is igneous, cemented grains are sedimentary, and squeezed warm solid rock is metamorphic. Two stops share the igneous target.

left.label: Lava crust cooled on a volcano slope
Sand grains cemented together in a lake bed
Buried clay layer squeezed and warmed without melting
Magma crystallized in an underground chamber

questions.prompt: Put this melting-route journey in order, from the buried rock to the last step.
questions.context: Reference diagram (simplified): melt must exist before it can rise, rise before it can cool in a new place, and the cooled rock must be exposed before weathering can reach it.
questions.explanation: Heating past melting makes magma, which rises and crystallizes. Only then can the new rock be exposed and weathered.

items.label: Buried rock is heated past its melting point
The resulting magma rises through a crack
Magma cools and crystallizes into igneous rock
Weathering breaks the exposed igneous rock into fragments

questions.prompt: Fork in the road: which route does your granite take next? Your choice sets the final question.
questions.context: Both routes are possible for this imaginary rock. Your pick is not graded; it decides which consequence question you get.
questions.explanation: Both routes are valid parts of the simplified rock cycle: surface rock can weather into sediment, and buried rock can melt. Your choice only picks the next trace.

options.label: Follow the river downhill as loose fragments
Sink into hot crust and melt

questions.prompt: River route: label the rock's state at each stop.
questions.context: Reference diagram (simplified): loose grains are sediment. Compacted and cemented layers become sedimentary rock. Deeper burial with warmth below melting and high pressure can make it metamorphic.
questions.explanation: Settled grains are sediment, cementing makes sedimentary rock, and deep warm squeezing of that solid rock makes metamorphic rock.

cells.label: Fragments settle on a lake bed
Thick layers press and cement the grains
That rock is buried deeper, warm but below melting, under high pressure

questions.prompt: Melting route: your magma erupts as lava and cools within hours. Which description fits the new rock?
questions.context: Reference diagram (simplified): slow cooling underground lets large crystals grow. Fast cooling at the surface leaves crystals tiny. Either way, cooled melt is igneous rock.
questions.explanation: Lava that cools in hours has little time to grow crystals, so the result is fine-grained igneous rock.

note: This road trip uses a simplified, invented rock-cycle model. Every rule, temperature and melting point is supplied in the question, so no outside geology knowledge is needed. Your fork choice is not graded and leads to one of two final questions.

title: Night Sky Clue Hunt
description: Tap clues on schematic sky diagrams to find what moves, what is lit and where things sit, then choose the explanation that fits the dated records.
note: Diagrams are simple schematics, not photos. Wanderers, notebooks, dates and the rise-time model in the cases are invented so every rule is given; the Moon questions follow NASA's public explanations.

sections.title: Tap the clue
sections.description: Five schematic sky diagrams.

sections.title: Choose the explanation
sections.description: Three short record-based cases.

questions.prompt: Tap the clue showing an object whose position changes against the fixed pattern across the three dates.
questions.context: Invented diagram, not a photo. Each box summarizes one kind of mark seen on Oct 1, Oct 8 and Oct 15 against a five-mark background pattern.
questions.explanation: Only a mark that shifts relative to the pattern from date to date is moving. Motion alone does not name the object; more dated frames would be needed.

diagram.title: Three dated frames, overlaid (invented)
diagram.description: Schematic panel with four boxes, each summarizing one mark's positions over Oct 1, Oct 8 and Oct 15.

zones.label: Pattern marks: identical positions on all three dates
One mark drifting steadily left to right across the pattern
A mark seen only on Oct 8, absent on the other dates
A mark at the same place each date, dimmer on Oct 15

options.label: Pattern marks, identical on all dates

questions.prompt: Sunlight arrives from the right. Tap the part of the Moon that makes up the phase we see.
questions.context: Schematic of the Moon as seen from Earth, with sunlight coming from the right. A gray strip below is drawn separately for comparison.
questions.explanation: A Moon phase is the sunlit portion of the Moon that we can see. It is not caused by Earth's shadow, which is a different event.

diagram.title: Moon disc lit from the right (schematic)
diagram.description: A Moon disc split into a left half and a right half, a gray strip below labeled as Earth's shadow, and a star-field band at the bottom.

zones.label: Right half of the disc: the sunlit side
Left half of the disc: the unlit side
Gray strip below: Earth's shadow, drawn apart from the Moon

questions.prompt: Tap where an object low over the western horizon would sit in this sketch.
questions.context: Invented notebook sketch: the observer faces south, so east is at the left and west at the right. The lower row is near the horizon; the upper row is high in the sky.
questions.explanation: Facing south puts west on the right. Low means the bottom row, so the right-hand bottom zone fits; the upper-right zone is western but high.

diagram.title: Sky sketch facing south (invented)
diagram.description: Four zones: low east at left, low south at center, low west at right, and a high zone on the western side.

questions.prompt: Tap the ruler mark where wanderer W should appear in week 4 if it keeps its steady pace.
questions.context: Invented log: W moves the same distance each week against the fixed pattern. Week 0 it sat at ruler mark 10, week 1 at mark 20, week 2 at mark 30.
questions.explanation: W gains 10 marks per week: 40 in week 3 and 50 in week 4. Mark 40 is the week 3 position, a common slip.

diagram.title: Ruler marks along the pattern (invented)
diagram.description: Four boxes left to right showing ruler marks 40, 50, 60 and 70.

questions.prompt: Tap the body whose shadow falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse.
questions.context: Schematic of the Sun, Earth and Moon in a straight line, not to scale. A dark band between Earth and Moon marks the shadow region.
questions.explanation: A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon moves into Earth's shadow. The dark band is the shadow itself, not the body casting it.

diagram.title: Sun, Earth and Moon in line (not to scale)
diagram.description: Left to right: Sun, Earth, a dark shadow band, then the Moon.

zones.label: Dark band between Earth and Moon: the shadow

questions.prompt: Which extra record would let this notebook call object K a slow wanderer?
questions.context: Invented notebook rule: call an object a slow wanderer only if it appears in at least three dated frames, shifting the same direction each time. K was recorded on Oct 1 and Oct 8, shifted rightward once.
questions.explanation: The rule needs a third dated frame with another rightward shift. Brightness, labels or a return to the start would not satisfy it.

options.label: A third dated frame with K shifted further rightward
A frame showing K looking brighter
A photo with a name label written on K
A frame with K back at its Oct 1 spot

questions.prompt: Using the model, when does the Lantern pattern rise on Night 6?
questions.context: Invented sky model: the Lantern pattern rises exactly 4 minutes earlier each night. On Night 1 it rises at 21:00.
questions.explanation: Night 6 is five nights after Night 1. Five steps of 4 minutes is 20 minutes earlier, giving 20:40.

questions.prompt: Which explanation best fits the two photos?
questions.context: Invented data: between photos, each of the five pattern marks shifted 3 units right. Mark W shifted 7 units right.
questions.explanation: Every pattern mark shifted together by 3, suggesting the view moved. W moved 4 units more than the pattern, so W also changed position relative to it.

options.label: Only W moved; the pattern stayed put
The view shifted by 3 units, and W moved 4 more against the pattern
All six marks moved independently of each other
W moved 7 units against the pattern
